title: FBI 'Most Wanted Fraudster' Manjit Bedi Returned From India in $600,000 SNAP Case
excerpt: The Kent grocery owner fled to India a week after pleading not guilty in April; arrested there in September, he is back in Washington to face wire fraud and food-stamp fraud charges.
body:
• Manjit Singh Bedi, 64, a Kent, Washington grocery owner on the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters list, was arrested by police in India in September and arrived back in the Western District of Washington on October 14.
  • Prosecutors allege he ran a cash-for-benefits scheme through his Tacoma store, The Asian Grocery Store, defrauding the SNAP food assistance programme of at least $600,000 between about March 2024 and June 2025.
  • Bedi was indicted in April, pleaded not guilty on April 22, and fled to India within a week; prosecutors will ask the court to detain him pending trial.
  • Wire fraud and SNAP fraud counts carry up to 20 years in prison each; he was due in US District Court in Tacoma on Friday.

A Washington state grocery store owner who fled to India after being indicted in an alleged $600,000 food-stamp fraud scheme has been returned to the United States to face charges, the US Justice Department announced, in a case the FBI is showcasing as proof that fugitives who run to their home countries are no longer out of reach.

The alleged scheme

Manjit Singh Bedi, 64, of Kent, owned The Asian Grocery Store in Tacoma. The indictment alleges that from about March 2024 to June 2025 he used beneficiaries' Electronic Benefit Transfer cards to ring up fraudulent food purchases, handed cardholders roughly half the value in cash and kept the rest — a classic trafficking pattern that converts food assistance into cash at a steep discount for the recipient and a profit for the store.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=fbXbPS_I_4w

"Stealing SNAP benefits — food assistance benefits intended for low-income Americans — is wrong and no matter where they run, we will not stop pursuing those who perpetrate these crimes."

— John Walk, USDA Inspector General

Flight, listing and arrest

Bedi was indicted for wire fraud in April and pleaded not guilty on April 22. Within a week, prosecutors say, he left for India. On September 3 he was placed on the FBI's new Most Wanted Fraudsters list, with a reward offered for information. Indian law enforcement took him into custody in September, and he was handed to federal agents, arriving in Washington on the night of October 14, according to the Justice Department. Officials have not said whether the transfer was a formal extradition or a deportation.

https://x.com/FBI/status/2110892088506065266

Acting US Attorney Neil Floyd said prosecutors will ask the court to detain Bedi pending trial, citing his demonstrated will and means to flee.

A broader fugitive push

FBI Director Kash Patel said Bedi is one of six Most Wanted Fraudsters captured since the list was created three months ago — a group accused of a combined $2 billion in fraud — and that the bureau has secured 260 extraditions and removals in 20 months, up more than 70% from the previous period. The American Bazaar reported he was scheduled to appear in the US District Court in Tacoma on Friday.

For South Asian store owners, the case is a pointed reminder that SNAP trafficking enforcement no longer stops at the border — and that a not-guilty plea followed by flight converts a defensible fraud case into a fugitive hunt with detention likely at the end of it. Bedi's allegations remain unproven; the charges will now be tested in court.
